steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Eamon Hale had kept watch at the northernmost point of Blackstone Head for nearly twenty years. Night after night he climbed the narrow spiral staircase, oil lamp in hand, to light the great Fresnel lens—and every morning before dawn he descended to feed the gulls and tend the weather log. The roar of the Atlantic battered the rocky shore below, but inside the lighthouse, Eamon found a calm purpose.

One wind-whipped evening in late October, a storm unlike any he’d seen swept in from the northeast. Waves towered against the granite cliffs, and lightning sketched the tumultuous sky. Eamon hurried through his ritual—polishing the glass, checking the mechanism, filling the lamp with fresh fuel—and then he settled at the window to watch. He felt less like a man in peril than a guardian in his fortress, steady amid chaos.

At the height of the gale, the tremor of thunder masked a faint distress signal. Eamon’s trained ear caught the dying Morse taps drifting through the roar. Without hesitation, he swung the lamp’s beam into a frantic, circular sweep, hoping to guide the unseen ship. Then he dashed to his radio, fingers trembling, and relayed the beacon’s coordinates to the rescue fleet. For nearly an hour he held the light steady, even as the wind threatened to extinguish it.

When the storm finally spent itself, dawn broke over a calm sea. On the jagged beach below lay a battered fishing cutter, its crew safe and shivering but alive. They waved up at Eamon, gratitude shining brighter than the rising sun. As he descended the stairs that morning, weary but proud, he realized the lonely tasks and constant vigilance were more than routine—they were a lifeline to sailors lost in the black. And so, come every dusk and dawn, Eamon Hale continued his watch, a steadfast keeper of hope at the edge of the world.
